title: Investigate life threatening hazards when handling animals

lessons.title: Identifying physical hazards in animal handling
lessons.html:
Animals can kill

Livestock handling causes serious injuries and deaths on South African farms every year. A bull, a cow protecting her calf, a frightened horse or an ostrich in breeding season can crush, gore, kick or trample a person in seconds. As a manager you must investigate these hazards, assess the risk and put controls in place. The OHS Act 85 of 1993 requires the employer to provide and maintain, as far as reasonably practicable, a working environment that is safe and without risk to employees' health.

Main physical hazards

HazardTypical situation
CrushingWorker caught between animal and crush, wall or gate
KicksStanding behind cattle or horses; milking parlours
Goring and buttingBulls, horned cattle, rams, buffalo on game farms
TramplingCattle rushing in a kraal or race
Bites and clawsPigs, horses, dogs, ostrich kicks
FallsSlippery races, climbing fences, horse riding
Vehicle incidentsHerding with bakkies, quad bikes or loading trucks

Behaviour as a hazard indicator

Understanding animal behaviour is the best prevention. Cattle have a wide field of vision but a blind spot directly behind them. They have a flight zone: enter it and they move away; enter too deep or too fast and they panic. Animals isolated from the herd, cows with newborn calves, bulls, animals in pain and animals handled roughly are most dangerous. Warning signs include head lowering, pawing, tail swishing, ears pinned back and snorting.

Investigating a site

Walk the handling facilities: are there escape gaps or man-gates in kraals and races? Is the crush in good repair with working head clamp and side gates? Are floors non-slip? Is lighting even, without shadows that make animals baulk? Record each hazard for the risk assessment.

lessons.title: Biological and chemical hazards
lessons.html:
Hazards you cannot see

Zoonotic diseases

Several animal diseases can infect and kill people.

  • Anthrax: sudden death of animals, sometimes with dark blood from openings. Never open the carcass; report to the state vet.
  • Rabies: spread by bites or saliva from infected dogs, jackals, cattle and other mammals. Any animal behaving strangely must be isolated and reported; a person bitten or exposed to saliva must wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water and get medical treatment urgently.
  • Brucellosis: from aborted material, afterbirths and raw milk. Wear gloves and do not drink raw milk from untested herds.
  • Rift Valley fever and Q fever: risk when handling aborting animals and tissues, especially after wet seasons.
  • Tuberculosis from infected cattle and raw milk.

Many of these are controlled under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984. Report suspicions to the state veterinarian.

Chemical hazards

Dips, pour-ons, dewormers, disinfectants and veterinary drugs are registered under Act 36 of 1947 or medicines legislation and can be toxic. Organophosphate dips, for example, can poison people through skin contact and inhalation.

  • Follow the label and safety data sheet for PPE: gloves, overalls, face protection.
  • Mix dip in ventilated areas, keep children and food away.
  • Never eat, drink or smoke while handling remedies; wash afterwards.
  • Store chemicals locked up and keep empty containers for approved disposal.

Needlestick injuries

Accidental self-injection of some vaccines and drugs can cause serious harm. Restrain animals properly before injecting, never carry uncapped needles, use sharps containers and seek medical help with the product label if injured.

lessons.title: Risk assessment and controls
lessons.html:
From hazard to control

Risk assessment steps

  1. Identify hazards by inspection, talking to workers and reviewing incident records.
  2. Decide who might be harmed and how.
  3. Rate the risk: how likely and how severe.
  4. Decide on controls using the hierarchy below.
  5. Record findings, train staff, and review after any incident or change.

Hierarchy of control

  • Eliminate: polled breeds or dehorning reduces goring; culling aggressive animals.
  • Engineer: well-designed curved races, solid sides, non-slip floors, working crushes and head clamps, man-gates and escape gaps, loading ramps at the right angle.
  • Administrative: safe work procedures, never working alone with bulls, training in low-stress handling, rotation to reduce fatigue, keeping children away.
  • PPE: safety boots, gloves, overalls, face protection for chemicals.

Safe handling rules

  • Always plan an escape route before entering a pen.
  • Move animals quietly using the flight zone and point of balance; do not shout or use sticks.
  • Never stand directly behind cattle or horses or in a race with animals.
  • Never enter a pen alone with a bull.
  • Do not put arms through crush bars where a moving animal can trap them.

Emergency preparedness

Have a first aid kit, a trained first aider, a charged phone and the nearest clinic and emergency numbers posted. In an emergency, ensure the scene is safe, call for help, and give first aid only within your training. Hands-on first aid training by an accredited provider is required. Investigate every incident and near-miss to stop it happening again.

Key points

  • Crushing, kicks, goring and trampling are the main physical hazards.
  • Zoonoses such as anthrax, rabies and brucellosis can kill people.
  • Use the hierarchy of control, starting with elimination and engineering.
  • Plan escape routes and never work alone with bulls.
  • Investigate incidents and near-misses.

quiz.question: Where is a cow's blind spot?

options.text: Directly in front of the nose

quiz.question: What should a person bitten by a suspected rabid animal do first?

options.text: Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water and get urgent medical treatment
Wait to see if symptoms develop
Cover the wound and continue working

options.text: Man-gates and escape gaps in kraals
